Below is a synthesis of evidence-backed approaches to employer branding, integrating definitions, frameworks, levers, tactics, and measurement. The recommendations connect established models to practical steps and outcomes, with attention to internal and external stakeholders and potential pitfalls.

What employer branding is and why it matters
- Employer branding applies marketing principles to talent attraction and retention by promoting a company’s distinctive attributes to internal and external audiences to stand out in competitive labor markets. <cite id="5548f702-0">Employer branding is a marketing-based approach to efficient recruitment and retention of qualified professionals that consists of promoting inside and outside the company the organization’s unique and desirable attributes; it is a prime response to recruitment and retention challenges and enhances employee motivation</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">It is a long-term strategy to attract and retain current and potential employees by promoting a distinctive and attractive employer image, with positive impacts on engagement and reduced turnover intention</cite>.
- Conceptually, it centers on the employer value proposition (EVP) and brand associations. <cite id="5548f702-0">The employer brand can be defined as the package of functional, economic, and psychological benefits identified with the company; employer branding covers developing the EVP, external marketing of the brand for recruitment, and internal marketing to build a committed workforce</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">EVP is the package of reward features and employment advantages and benefits offered to employees and must be linked to the corporate brand’s central message</cite>.
- Employer branding is tied to outcomes across the value chain. <cite id="5548f702-0">It helps enhance employee motivation and strengthens organizational identity and belonging</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Strong employer brands improve applicant attraction and recruitment efficiency and raise engagement and commitment while reducing turnover intention</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Evidence shows positive effects on expected pride from membership, applicant pool quantity and quality, and firm performance advantages</cite>.

Core frameworks and process approaches
- Three-step process to anchor strategy. <cite id="5548f702-0">Employer branding comprises three core aspects: developing the employer value proposition, externally marketing the brand to target audiences for recruitment, and internally marketing the brand to build a committed, retained workforce</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">First, develop a concept of value for prospective and current employees (EVP) grounded in an image audit; second, externally market the proposition to attract targets; third, internalize the promise by embedding it in organizational culture</cite>.
- Brand equity-based value chain and integrative models. <cite id="5548f702-3">An integrative model clarifies elements, scope, and outcomes of employer branding programs for different stakeholders, illustrates interrelations across stages, and provides levers to develop effective recruiting and retaining strategies</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-2">Given conceptual ambiguity, an integrative model and analytical three-step process are proposed toward sustainable organization</cite>.
- Positioning relative to competitors. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">EVP development should emphasize relative positioning across target groups and competitive contexts; points-of-parity without points-of-difference lack brand differentiation, and unique, favorable brand associations drive differential applicant and employee responses</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">A distinctive EVP adds impetus to the employer brand, motivates candidates to join and current employees to stay, and enables targeted employer brand marketing</cite>.
- Stakeholder perceptions and authenticity. <cite id="5548f702-1">Employer branding uses branding assessment metrics to understand how stakeholders perceive the company and guides strategic decisions; authenticity of company values is decisive for employees’ opinions</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Employer branding communicates organizational values to stakeholders and helps candidates assess fit, with both instrumental (pay, career) and symbolic (warm, innovative) attributes shaping attractiveness</cite>.

Implementation approaches across the value chain
1) Diagnose and audit the “great place to work” identity
- Build the EVP from a comprehensive image audit. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">The EVP should derive from a thorough audit of characteristics that make the firm an attractive employer, and image audits underpin the subsequent steps</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-3">Employer branding research highlights organizational inputs, outcomes, and interrelations, supporting decision-making with an enhanced view of applicant/employee attitudes and behaviors</cite>.
- Map attributes and points of difference. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Differentiation requires identifying unique, favorable attributes relative to candidate segments and competitors; without distinctive points-of-difference, the proposition lacks brand value</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Image audits should incorporate stakeholder beliefs about attractive-employer characteristics and can be tailored across labor pool, applicants, and current employees</cite>.

2) External employer branding to attract the right audience
- Craft and communicate the EVP with clarity and consistency. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">EVP content must be linked to the corporate brand’s central message to create a convincing proposition</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Consistency and clarity of the proposition affect favorable perception, and relative positioning across segments matters</cite>.
- Use early recruitment practices and channels. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">External marketing can be executed through early recruitment practices that shape the employer image and attract target populations</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Traditional recruitment metrics (e.g., time to fill, quality of hire, cost per hire) and candidate-side metrics (e.g., application completion, callback) are commonly used to evaluate recruitment performance</cite>.
- Align content with what drives attraction. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Employer attractiveness is shaped by explicit information (job descriptions) and informal information (recruitment experience), making the recruitment process vital for employer image formation</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">Instrumental (rewards), symbolic (culture-fit), and functional (work design) attributes are perceived by candidates and influence intention to apply</cite>.
- Integrate the candidate experience into branding. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Modern recruitment measurement increasingly links marketing media to applications and quality hires, and calls for integrating brand reputation and experience; employer brand metrics are important because of the benefits in attraction and retention</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-4">Employer branding impacts behaviors such as applying, interviewing, accepting offers, and recommending the company, which improve applicant quantity and quality</cite>.

3) Internal employer branding to recruit, engage, and retain
- Internalize the promise in culture, values, and leadership. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">The third step carries the brand promise into organizational culture and internal marketing to build an engaged workforce</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Promoting an employer brand internally communicates values and helps employees evaluate fit; strong internal employer branding improves engagement, commitment, and reduces turnover intention</cite>.
- Link pay, career, and psychological contracts to identity. <cite id="5548f702-0">The set of tangible and intangible employer attributes enhances organizational belonging and identification among acquired employees who have an exclusive and outstanding employment experience</cite>.
- Close the loop with leadership and work design. <cite id="5548f702-1">Leadership, job design, recognition, work environment, and growth opportunities influence engagement and satisfaction and pivot the organization’s employer branding</cite>.

4) Messaging, storytelling, and channels
- Define brand associations and tailor to segments. <cite id="5548f702-1">Brand associations define stakeholders’ perceptions; many are influenced by factors beyond direct control, underscoring the need to manage messaging and positioning</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Prioritizing relative employer image attributes by candidate segments yields more effective strategies</cite>.
- Communicate both instrumental and symbolic attributes. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Instrumental (e.g., pay, career opportunities) and symbolic (e.g., warm, innovative) attributes combine to shape employer attractiveness</cite>.
- Use integrated communication across the candidate journey. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Recruitment experience acts as informal information that shapes employer image, so the process itself is a branding lever</cite>.

Measuring impact and managing performance
- Recruitment-side KPIs to validate attraction effectiveness. <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Common measures include acceptance rate, quality of hire, efficiency ratio, candidate and manager satisfaction, cost per hire, time to fill, retention rate, application completion, callback rate, candidates per hire, fill rate, turnover rate, response rate, qualified candidates per opening, funnel effectiveness, productivity of new employees, selection ratio, and offer acceptance rate</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-4">Employer branding orientation relates to improved recruitment performance and recruitment satisfaction</cite>.
- Quality of applicants and fit. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">A differentiated EVP motivates target candidates to join and current employees to stay, linking brand distinctiveness to talent attraction and retention</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">EVP as a measure of employer attractiveness is grounded in constructs that connect to intention to apply and early-stage applicant outcomes</cite>.
- Candidate experience and employer reputation. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Evaluations increasingly integrate brand reputation and experience with media-driven sources to understand links to applications and quality hires</cite>.
- Employee outcomes as lag indicators. <cite id="5548f702-4">Strong employer brands improve engagement and commitment and reduce turnover intention, providing lag indicators of internal branding success</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Evidence also links employer branding to expected pride from membership and firm performance advantages</cite>.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Misalignment between brand and day-to-day experience. <cite id="5548f702-1">Authenticity of company values is decisive for employees’ opinions; strategies must align with real behaviors and reputation</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Employer branding communicates values and fit; misalignment risks erode credibility with employees and candidates</cite>.
- Overemphasis on external image without internal foundation. <cite id="5548f702-4">Research notes that external branding has dominated attention while internal employer branding remains underexplored but critical for employee attitudes and retention</cite>.
- Generic EVPs lacking differentiation. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Overlaps with competitors (points-of-parity) without distinctive attributes yield no differentiation; firms should identify unique associations that drive differential responses</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Image audits should capture relative importance of attributes across potential applicants, actual applicants, and current employees to avoid one-size-fits-all mis-specification</cite>.
- Relying on static messaging rather than experience. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Candidate perceptions form during the recruitment process; integrating branding into the process and experience improves employer image</cite>.

Actionable approaches to build and manage your employer brand
1) Diagnose and differentiate
- Run a multi-stakeholder image audit to identify what makes you distinctive. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Ground the EVP in an image audit that surfaces attributes and beliefs about what makes the firm an attractive employer</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Tailor the audit across general labor pool, applicants, and current employees to capture different beliefs and priorities</cite>.
- Translate findings into a clear EVP with points-of-parity and points-of-difference. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Only attributes that are both favorable and unique create differential responses; emphasize relative importance across segments</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Distinctive EVPs motivate joining and staying</cite>.

2) Design the value chain: attract, convert, and retain
- Attract: craft compelling narratives and content around instrumental and symbolic attributes; optimize early recruitment practices and candidate experience. <cite id="5548f702-4">Promoting an employer brand externally can establish an employer of choice and enable attraction of the best candidates</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Early recruitment practices can market the employer brand</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">Instrumental, symbolic, and functional attributes shape perceived attractiveness and intention to apply</cite>.
- Convert: ensure the offer and onboarding promise match the brand. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Carry the brand promise into organizational culture and internal marketing to build an engaged workforce</cite>.
- Retain: reinforce identity, belonging, and growth through leadership, recognition, and career development. <cite id="5548f702-0">Tangible and intangible attributes enhance organizational belonging and identification among employees</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-1">Leadership, job design, recognition, work environment, and growth opportunities drive engagement and satisfaction, pivoting employer branding</cite>.

3) Execute with integrated tactics
- Messaging and content: articulate a consistent EVP linked to corporate brand; tailor to segments; combine instrumental and symbolic stories. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Link EVP content to the corporate brand’s central message</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Relative positioning and clarity/consistency improve perception</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Symbolic and instrumental attributes jointly shape attractiveness</cite>.
- Channels and experience: optimize job boards, career site UX, employer branding content, and recruitment process touchpoints to reinforce the brand promise. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Recruitment experience is a major informal information source shaping employer image</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Data-driven recruitment increasingly links media and candidate experience to applications and quality hires</cite>.
- Employee voice and culture: enable employee advocacy and authentic storytelling aligned with brand values. <cite id="5548f702-1">Authenticity of values is decisive for employees’ opinions; employee engagement and satisfaction are central to employer branding</cite>.

4) Measure and iterate
- Set a balanced scorecard: recruitment efficiency (time to fill, cost per hire, quality of hire, efficiency ratio), applicant quality and fit, candidate satisfaction/experience, and employee outcomes (engagement, commitment, turnover intention). <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Use established recruitment metrics to evaluate performance</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Link employer branding programs to improved recruitment performance and satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Track engagement, commitment, and turnover intention as lag indicators</cite>.
- Diagnose misalignments through audits and candidate feedback. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Integrate brand reputation and experience into measurement to detect gaps between messaging and perceived reality</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Use segment-specific beliefs to refine the EVP and tactics</cite>.
- Iterate the model: use data to refine EVP, optimize channels, and strengthen internalization. <cite id="5548f702-3">Integrative models provide levers and interrelations to guide continuous improvement in employer branding programs</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical step-by-step
- Step 1: Stakeholder audit and discovery. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Interview potential applicants, actual applicants, and current employees to identify attributes they value and the relative importance across groups</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Identify points-of-parity and points-of-difference to ensure differentiation</cite>.
- Step 2: Define the EVP and brand promise. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Craft an EVP linked to the corporate brand’s central message</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Position the EVP relative to target segments and competitors, ensuring unique favorable associations</cite>.
- Step 3: Build the value chain. <cite id="5548f702-0">Develop external marketing to attract (recruitment task) and internal marketing to retain and commit</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Implement early recruitment practices and embed the promise in culture</cite>.
- Step 4: Execute across channels and experience. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Align job descriptions, recruitment interactions, and portals with EVP; leverage the recruitment process as a brand touchpoint</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-1">Use social and content channels with authentic, value-aligned messaging</cite>.
- Step 5: Measure and close the loop. <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Track recruitment metrics (quality of hire, time to fill, cost per hire, candidate satisfaction) and retention/engagement outcomes</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Use intent-to-apply, application quality, engagement, and turnover intention as behavioral indicators</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Integrate employer reputation and candidate experience to detect misalignments and guide refinements</cite>.

Context and boundary conditions
- Evidence strength and gaps. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">While causal studies are limited, multiple studies converge on positive links from employer branding to applicant behaviors and recruitment outcomes, and to engagement/retention and firm performance</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">More empirical work exists on external employer branding than on internal employer branding, but the internal side clearly affects employee attitudes</cite>.
- Sector adaptations. <cite id="5548f702-1">Employer branding is shaped by the role of corporate and external influencers (e.g., for Gen Z), and strategies can be tailored by target group</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Mission-driven organizations can use values and purpose (e.g., peacekeeping, humanitarian roles) as salient brand attributes in recruitment</cite>.

In sum, effective employer branding is a coherent, data-informed program that begins with a rigorous image audit, defines a differentiated EVP, communicates consistently across recruitment and employee experiences, and is managed with balanced metrics that link attraction quality to retention and engagement outcomes. <cite id="5548f702-0">Employer branding integrates marketing-based external recruitment and internal commitment-building to stand out in competitive labor markets</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-3">Integrative models and brand equity perspectives offer practical levers and outcome linkages to guide strategy and execution</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-1">Authenticity and alignment with real organizational values and experiences are critical to credibility and impact</cite>.

Title: Employer branding: A brand equity-based literature review and research agenda
Snippet: The first stage of the model is concerned with what firms can do to develop (potential) employees' employer knowledge. Prior conceptualizations broadly described this step as employer branding, i.e. a threestep process composed of (i) the development of an EVP that includes the key message of the brand, (ii) the external marketing of the value proposition to its target group(s), and (iii) the internal marketing of the employer brand to build an engaged workforce based on firm values and goals (Backhaus and Tikoo 2004;Edwards 2010). An EVP can be understood as a desired or ideal employer identity, i.e. how the company wants to be perceived by (potential) employees as an attractive employer.

We refine and extend this first stage of employer branding in at least three important ways. First, with regard to EVP development, prior views were concerned primarily with the identification of relevant EVP elements that create favorable employee attitudes (e.g. instrumental-symbolic image attributes; Gowan 2004;). In contrast, we propose that future research needs to focus much more on relative EVP development, i.e. how the EVP should be positioned or modified with regard to diverse target groups and therefore different applicant/employee segments of a company (e.g. external vs. internal candidates, blue collar vs. white collar; Avery and McKay 2006).

Below is a synthesis of evidence-backed approaches to employer branding, integrating definitions, frameworks, levers, tactics, and measurement. The recommendations connect established models to practical steps and outcomes, with attention to internal and external stakeholders and potential pitfalls.

What employer branding is and why it matters
- Employer branding applies marketing principles to talent attraction and retention by promoting a company’s distinctive attributes to internal and external audiences to stand out in competitive labor markets. <cite id="5548f702-0">Employer branding is a marketing-based approach to efficient recruitment and retention of qualified professionals that consists of promoting inside and outside the company the organization’s unique and desirable attributes; it is a prime response to recruitment and retention challenges and enhances employee motivation</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">It is a long-term strategy to attract and retain current and potential employees by promoting a distinctive and attractive employer image, with positive impacts on engagement and reduced turnover intention</cite>.
- Conceptually, it centers on the employer value proposition (EVP) and brand associations. <cite id="5548f702-0">The employer brand can be defined as the package of functional, economic, and psychological benefits identified with the company; employer branding covers developing the EVP, external marketing of the brand for recruitment, and internal marketing to build a committed workforce</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">EVP is the package of reward features and employment advantages and benefits offered to employees and must be linked to the corporate brand’s central message</cite>.
- Employer branding is tied to outcomes across the value chain. <cite id="5548f702-0">It helps enhance employee motivation and strengthens organizational identity and belonging</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Strong employer brands improve applicant attraction and recruitment efficiency and raise engagement and commitment while reducing turnover intention</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Evidence shows positive effects on expected pride from membership, applicant pool quantity and quality, and firm performance advantages</cite>.

Core frameworks and process approaches
- Three-step process to anchor strategy. <cite id="5548f702-0">Employer branding comprises three core aspects: developing the employer value proposition, externally marketing the brand to target audiences for recruitment, and internally marketing the brand to build a committed, retained workforce</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">First, develop a concept of value for prospective and current employees (EVP) grounded in an image audit; second, externally market the proposition to attract targets; third, internalize the promise by embedding it in organizational culture</cite>.
- Brand equity-based value chain and integrative models. <cite id="5548f702-3">An integrative model clarifies elements, scope, and outcomes of employer branding programs for different stakeholders, illustrates interrelations across stages, and provides levers to develop effective recruiting and retaining strategies</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-2">Given conceptual ambiguity, an integrative model and analytical three-step process are proposed toward sustainable organization</cite>.
- Positioning relative to competitors. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">EVP development should emphasize relative positioning across target groups and competitive contexts; points-of-parity without points-of-difference lack brand differentiation, and unique, favorable brand associations drive differential applicant and employee responses</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">A distinctive EVP adds impetus to the employer brand, motivates candidates to join and current employees to stay, and enables targeted employer brand marketing</cite>.
- Stakeholder perceptions and authenticity. <cite id="5548f702-1">Employer branding uses branding assessment metrics to understand how stakeholders perceive the company and guides strategic decisions; authenticity of company values is decisive for employees’ opinions</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Employer branding communicates organizational values to stakeholders and helps candidates assess fit, with both instrumental (pay, career) and symbolic (warm, innovative) attributes shaping attractiveness</cite>.

Implementation approaches across the value chain
1) Diagnose and audit the “great place to work” identity
- Build the EVP from a comprehensive image audit. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">The EVP should derive from a thorough audit of characteristics that make the firm an attractive employer, and image audits underpin the subsequent steps</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-3">Employer branding research highlights organizational inputs, outcomes, and interrelations, supporting decision-making with an enhanced view of applicant/employee attitudes and behaviors</cite>.
- Map attributes and points of difference. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Differentiation requires identifying unique, favorable attributes relative to candidate segments and competitors; without distinctive points-of-difference, the proposition lacks brand value</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Image audits should incorporate stakeholder beliefs about attractive-employer characteristics and can be tailored across labor pool, applicants, and current employees</cite>.

2) External employer branding to attract the right audience
- Craft and communicate the EVP with clarity and consistency. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">EVP content must be linked to the corporate brand’s central message to create a convincing proposition</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Consistency and clarity of the proposition affect favorable perception, and relative positioning across segments matters</cite>.
- Use early recruitment practices and channels. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">External marketing can be executed through early recruitment practices that shape the employer image and attract target populations</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Traditional recruitment metrics (e.g., time to fill, quality of hire, cost per hire) and candidate-side metrics (e.g., application completion, callback) are commonly used to evaluate recruitment performance</cite>.
- Align content with what drives attraction. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Employer attractiveness is shaped by explicit information (job descriptions) and informal information (recruitment experience), making the recruitment process vital for employer image formation</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">Instrumental (rewards), symbolic (culture-fit), and functional (work design) attributes are perceived by candidates and influence intention to apply</cite>.
- Integrate the candidate experience into branding. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Modern recruitment measurement increasingly links marketing media to applications and quality hires, and calls for integrating brand reputation and experience; employer brand metrics are important because of the benefits in attraction and retention</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-4">Employer branding impacts behaviors such as applying, interviewing, accepting offers, and recommending the company, which improve applicant quantity and quality</cite>.

3) Internal employer branding to recruit, engage, and retain
- Internalize the promise in culture, values, and leadership. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">The third step carries the brand promise into organizational culture and internal marketing to build an engaged workforce</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Promoting an employer brand internally communicates values and helps employees evaluate fit; strong internal employer branding improves engagement, commitment, and reduces turnover intention</cite>.
- Link pay, career, and psychological contracts to identity. <cite id="5548f702-0">The set of tangible and intangible employer attributes enhances organizational belonging and identification among acquired employees who have an exclusive and outstanding employment experience</cite>.
- Close the loop with leadership and work design. <cite id="5548f702-1">Leadership, job design, recognition, work environment, and growth opportunities influence engagement and satisfaction and pivot the organization’s employer branding</cite>.

4) Messaging, storytelling, and channels
- Define brand associations and tailor to segments. <cite id="5548f702-1">Brand associations define stakeholders’ perceptions; many are influenced by factors beyond direct control, underscoring the need to manage messaging and positioning</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Prioritizing relative employer image attributes by candidate segments yields more effective strategies</cite>.
- Communicate both instrumental and symbolic attributes. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Instrumental (e.g., pay, career opportunities) and symbolic (e.g., warm, innovative) attributes combine to shape employer attractiveness</cite>.
- Use integrated communication across the candidate journey. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Recruitment experience acts as informal information that shapes employer image, so the process itself is a branding lever</cite>.

Measuring impact and managing performance
- Recruitment-side KPIs to validate attraction effectiveness. <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Common measures include acceptance rate, quality of hire, efficiency ratio, candidate and manager satisfaction, cost per hire, time to fill, retention rate, application completion, callback rate, candidates per hire, fill rate, turnover rate, response rate, qualified candidates per opening, funnel effectiveness, productivity of new employees, selection ratio, and offer acceptance rate</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-4">Employer branding orientation relates to improved recruitment performance and recruitment satisfaction</cite>.
- Quality of applicants and fit. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">A differentiated EVP motivates target candidates to join and current employees to stay, linking brand distinctiveness to talent attraction and retention</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">EVP as a measure of employer attractiveness is grounded in constructs that connect to intention to apply and early-stage applicant outcomes</cite>.
- Candidate experience and employer reputation. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Evaluations increasingly integrate brand reputation and experience with media-driven sources to understand links to applications and quality hires</cite>.
- Employee outcomes as lag indicators. <cite id="5548f702-4">Strong employer brands improve engagement and commitment and reduce turnover intention, providing lag indicators of internal branding success</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Evidence also links employer branding to expected pride from membership and firm performance advantages</cite>.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Misalignment between brand and day-to-day experience. <cite id="5548f702-1">Authenticity of company values is decisive for employees’ opinions; strategies must align with real behaviors and reputation</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Employer branding communicates values and fit; misalignment risks erode credibility with employees and candidates</cite>.
- Overemphasis on external image without internal foundation. <cite id="5548f702-4">Research notes that external branding has dominated attention while internal employer branding remains underexplored but critical for employee attitudes and retention</cite>.
- Generic EVPs lacking differentiation. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Overlaps with competitors (points-of-parity) without distinctive attributes yield no differentiation; firms should identify unique associations that drive differential responses</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Image audits should capture relative importance of attributes across potential applicants, actual applicants, and current employees to avoid one-size-fits-all mis-specification</cite>.
- Relying on static messaging rather than experience. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Candidate perceptions form during the recruitment process; integrating branding into the process and experience improves employer image</cite>.

Actionable approaches to build and manage your employer brand
1) Diagnose and differentiate
- Run a multi-stakeholder image audit to identify what makes you distinctive. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Ground the EVP in an image audit that surfaces attributes and beliefs about what makes the firm an attractive employer</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Tailor the audit across general labor pool, applicants, and current employees to capture different beliefs and priorities</cite>.
- Translate findings into a clear EVP with points-of-parity and points-of-difference. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Only attributes that are both favorable and unique create differential responses; emphasize relative importance across segments</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Distinctive EVPs motivate joining and staying</cite>.

2) Design the value chain: attract, convert, and retain
- Attract: craft compelling narratives and content around instrumental and symbolic attributes; optimize early recruitment practices and candidate experience. <cite id="5548f702-4">Promoting an employer brand externally can establish an employer of choice and enable attraction of the best candidates</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Early recruitment practices can market the employer brand</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-1">Instrumental, symbolic, and functional attributes shape perceived attractiveness and intention to apply</cite>.
- Convert: ensure the offer and onboarding promise match the brand. <cite id="4bb8cec4-3">Carry the brand promise into organizational culture and internal marketing to build an engaged workforce</cite>.
- Retain: reinforce identity, belonging, and growth through leadership, recognition, and career development. <cite id="5548f702-0">Tangible and intangible attributes enhance organizational belonging and identification among employees</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-1">Leadership, job design, recognition, work environment, and growth opportunities drive engagement and satisfaction, pivoting employer branding</cite>.

3) Execute with integrated tactics
- Messaging and content: articulate a consistent EVP linked to corporate brand; tailor to segments; combine instrumental and symbolic stories. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Link EVP content to the corporate brand’s central message</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Relative positioning and clarity/consistency improve perception</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">Symbolic and instrumental attributes jointly shape attractiveness</cite>.
- Channels and experience: optimize job boards, career site UX, employer branding content, and recruitment process touchpoints to reinforce the brand promise. <cite id="4bb8cec4-0">Recruitment experience is a major informal information source shaping employer image</cite>. <cite id="cf3d6744-0">Data-driven recruitment increasingly links media and candidate experience to applications and quality hires</cite>.
- Employee voice and culture: enable employee advocacy and authentic storytelling aligned with brand values. <cite id="5548f702-1">Authenticity of values is decisive for employees’ opinions; employee engagement and satisfaction are central to employer branding</cite>.

4) Measure and iterate
- Set a balanced scorecard: recruitment efficiency (time to fill, cost per hire, quality of hire, efficiency ratio), applicant quality and fit, candidate satisfaction/experience, and employee outcomes (engagement, commitment, turnover intention). <cite id="cf3d6744-1">Use established recruitment metrics to evaluate performance</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Link employer branding programs to improved recruitment performance and satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">Track engagement, commitment, and turnover intention as lag indicators</cite>.

- Iterate the model: use data to refine EVP, optimize channels, and strengthen internalization. <cite id="5548f702-3">Integrative models provide levers and interrelations to guide continuous improvement in employer branding programs</cite>.

- Step 1: Stakeholder audit and discovery. <cite id="cf3d6744-3">Interview potential applicants, actual applicants, and current employees to identify attributes they value and the relative importance across groups</cite>. <cite id="4bb8cec4-2">Identify points-of-parity and points-of-difference to ensure differentiation</cite>.

- Evidence strength and gaps. <cite id="4bb8cec4-4">While causal studies are limited, multiple studies converge on positive links from employer branding to applicant behaviors and recruitment outcomes, and to engagement/retention and firm performance</cite>. <cite id="5548f702-4">More empirical work exists on external employer branding than on internal employer branding, but the internal side clearly affects employee attitudes</cite>.

Summary
Employer branding (EB) typically improves attraction—but it can worsen talent attraction outcomes when organizations over-identify “what is attractive” with generic prestige or culture, misrepresent or inauthentically sell an incoherent value proposition, fail to differentiate by job, or target audiences without segmenting for context and market conditions. The mechanisms include halo-based inferences from overall employer attractiveness to specific job fit, transfer‑appropriate processing failures, expectation‑state distortions under scarcity, and homogenization of applicant pools; these risks intensify when internal practices do not align with the externally communicated brand and when messages are not tailored to labor market constraints and cultural segments. <cite id="b318d47e-0">Companies are often ineffective in developing, maintaining or realigning employer brand efforts, thereby losing out on a powerful tool for talent attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="43896364-0">A growing body of evidence links employer brand to attraction and retention, yet many firms mis-specify or misalign their EB programs</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Employer attractiveness influences employer choices and retention through candidate appraisals of signs such as prestige and culture, and sector context shapes those signals</cite>.

When EB initiatives worsen talent attraction outcomes
1) Halo/representativeness from “attractiveness” to specific job fit, without job differentiation
- Halo effect and representative heuristics: Candidates infer job appeal from general organizational attractiveness cues (prestige, innovation, culture), and then apply broadly; if these cues do not match a particular role’s requirements, EB can lure quantity without quality. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Attractiveness factors such as prestige, innovation, and culture serve as signals in applicants’ appraisal of the job, employer, and decision to apply</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-1">Employer attractiveness is differentiated in functional, economic, and psychological benefits, but many programs emphasize image without tying to concrete, role-relevant value</cite>.
- Transfer-appropriate processing failure: EB content that is compelling but not role-specific fails to build discriminators that predict who will perform well on the actual job. <cite id="43896364-2">Key EB building blocks—segmented target needs, a differentiated EVP, people management strategy, brand consistency, communication, and HR metrics—are needed to predict attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="43896364-3">An integrated approach is required where employer attractiveness is shaped to attract and retain talent, not an aggregate image divorced from job differentiation</cite>.

2) Misrepresentation and cover-up (inauthenticity), undermining trust and fit
- Social desirability and cover-up: If EB overemphasizes “positive” culture/salary cues without authenticity, candidates discount the brand and may avoid applying or exit quickly. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Employees perceive employer attractiveness from success, alignment with product/service values, and an attractive external image; these perceptions are culturally biased, and strong EB can generate internal side effects</cite> <cite id="43896364-2">Brand consistency and an authentic differentiated EVP are core building blocks; their absence invites skepticism</cite>.
- Expectation–reality gaps: EB promises prestige or flexible hours but internal practices do not match; candidates who accept offers then de‑motivate or depart. <cite id="b318d47e-0">Organizations that incorrectly realign EB efforts lose the attraction/retention tool, suggesting inauthentic or mismatched positioning erodes EB’s gains</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants use corporate reputation and talent management signals to appraise jobs; mismanagement of these signals reduces intention to apply</cite>.

3) Overemphasis on prestige/culture without concrete “value proposition to the candidate”
- Signaling theory in reverse: EB that markets culture or prestige as the main hook attracts candidates who fit the narrative but lack the skills or motivation for the role, diluting quality and speed-to-fill. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Prestige and innovation are salient attractiveness factors, yet sector and context moderate their appeal</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-1">EB is differentiated attractiveness in functional, economic, and psychological benefits, yet many programs lack coherent linkage to specific benefits candidates need</cite>.
- Practical implication: Over-identification with “cool culture” can widen gender/ethnic gaps if cues favor homogeneous referents. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and organizational culture act as signals that shape attraction; public vs. private and nonprofit contexts differ, affecting applicant pools</cite> <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity of EB activities matters; perceived external image influences attraction and internal job satisfaction</cite>.

4) Expectation-state dynamics under tight labor markets
- Under scarcity, generic EB can raise overall applications but compress the pool into overqualified, overpaid aspirants who reject offers or expect unreasonably high bundles. <cite id="b318d47e-4">With talent supply increasingly on the demand curve, EB is an enticement to attract scarce talent, but misalignment leaves effective attraction elusive</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-0">Firms that misalign EB in tight markets lose to competitors who correctly realign, worsening attraction outcomes</cite>.
- Under scarcity, EB that emphasizes prestige or “status” can inflame expectation gaps: candidates who perceive a “dream job” push back on compensation or timing, increasing time-to-fill and offer decay. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants use signals—prestige, reputation, sector—to appraise fit and decide to apply; misaligned signals in tight markets can reduce effective applications</cite>.

5) Poor internal–external alignment (people management, EVP coherence)
- EB as a front-office projection without back-office parity weakens attraction: candidates who join discover misfit in management, development, or reward, reducing retention and reputation spillovers. <cite id="43896364-2">People management strategy and a differentiated EVP are foundational building blocks; ignoring them reduces predictive validity for attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-0">Organizations that fail to realign EB with internal realities lose the powerful attraction/retention tool, indicating that misalignment undermines outcomes</cite>.
- Cultural context and generational shifts: EB content that fits one culture or cohort can turn off others, leading to narrower pools and missed targets. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity is needed; EB effectiveness depends on accuracy and appeal that varies by audience</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-4">Understanding what appeals to job searchers is crucial in severe talent shortages; attractiveness and accuracy determine EB success</cite>.

Why these mechanisms cause harm
- Halo/transfer failure: Candidates infer job desirability from general employer attractiveness (e.g., innovative culture) but the specific role requires analytical rigor or compliance; the EB-driven “fit” is misdirected, producing lower quality applicants and slower conversion to hires. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants’ attraction decisions rely on attractiveness factors like prestige and innovation</cite> <cite id="43896364-3">Attraction requires integrating building blocks so that employer attractiveness is tailored and job‑linked</cite>.
- Inauthenticity and skepticism: Perceived cover-up reduces internal credibility and external trust; candidates discount promises and avoid applying when they detect hypocrisy between EB and lived experience. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Perceived external image and cultural alignment drive attractiveness; misalignment can backfire</cite> <cite id="43896364-2">Brand consistency and a differentiated, credible EVP are core</cite>.
- Expectation-state distortion: In tight markets, generic EB can raise de‑sired applications from overqualified aspirants who expect premium bundles; when offers are rejected or bundles are constrained, time-to-fill and attrition worsen. <cite id="b318d47e-4">EB is an enticement in tight markets but effective attraction remains elusive without alignment</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and signal content shape attraction decisions, so misaligned EB under scarcity reduces effective applications</cite>.
- Homogenization and diversity risks: EB that emphasizes “cool culture” or sector cachet can attract similar, highly filtered cohorts, narrowing diversity and reducing functional fit for specialized roles. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and culture act as signals; attraction to the public vs. private sector differs</cite> <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity and audience-specific appeal are necessary; inattention increases risk of biased pools</cite>.

- Market tightness and talent scarcity: Tight markets amplify both the upside and downside of EB—more applications at greater cost, with higher risks of expectation gaps and de‑motivation if EB overpromises or lacks specificity. <cite id="b318d47e-4">EB’s enticement role intensifies under tight markets, yet many firms still struggle with effective attraction</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-0">Organizations that fail to realign EB under scarcity lose the talent race</cite>.

When EB initiatives worsen talent attraction outcomes
1) Halo/representativeness from “attractiveness” to specific job fit, without job differentiation
- Halo effect and representative heuristics: Candidates infer job appeal from general organizational attractiveness cues (prestige, innovation, culture), and then apply broadly; if these cues do not match a particular role’s requirements, EB can lure quantity without quality. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Attractiveness factors such as prestige, innovation, and culture serve as signals in applicants’ appraisal of the job, employer, and decision to apply</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-1">Employer attractiveness is differentiated in functional, economic, and psychological benefits, but many programs emphasize image without tying to concrete, role-relevant value</cite>.

2) Misrepresentation and cover-up (inauthenticity), undermining trust and fit
- Social desirability and cover-up: If EB overemphasizes “positive” culture/salary cues without authenticity, candidates discount the brand and may avoid applying or exit quickly. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Employees perceive employer attractiveness from success, alignment with product/service values, and an attractive external image; these perceptions are culturally biased, and strong EB can generate internal side effects</cite> <cite id="43896364-2">Brand consistency and an authentic differentiated EVP are core building blocks; their absence invites skepticism</cite>.
- Expectation–reality gaps: EB promises prestige or flexible hours but internal practices do not match; candidates who accept offers then de‑motivate or depart. <cite id="b318d47e-0">Organizations that incorrectly realign EB efforts lose the attraction/retention tool, suggesting inauthentic or mismatched positioning erodes EB’s gains</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants use corporate reputation and talent management signals to appraise jobs; mismanagement of these signals reduces intention to apply</cite>.

3) Overemphasis on prestige/culture without concrete “value proposition to the candidate”
- Signaling theory in reverse: EB that markets culture or prestige as the main hook attracts candidates who fit the narrative but lack the skills or motivation for the role, diluting quality and speed-to-fill. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Prestige and innovation are salient attractiveness factors, yet sector and context moderate their appeal</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-1">EB is differentiated attractiveness in functional, economic, and psychological benefits, yet many programs lack coherent linkage to specific benefits candidates need</cite>.
- Practical implication: Over-identification with “cool culture” can widen gender/ethnic gaps if cues favor homogeneous referents. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and organizational culture act as signals that shape attraction; public vs. private and nonprofit contexts differ, affecting applicant pools</cite> <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity of EB activities matters; perceived external image influences attraction and internal job satisfaction</cite>.

4) Expectation-state dynamics under tight labor markets
- Under scarcity, generic EB can raise overall applications but compress the pool into overqualified, overpaid aspirants who reject offers or expect unreasonably high bundles. <cite id="b318d47e-4">With talent supply increasingly on the demand curve, EB is an enticement to attract scarce talent, but misalignment leaves effective attraction elusive</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-0">Firms that misalign EB in tight markets lose to competitors who correctly realign, worsening attraction outcomes</cite>.

5) Poor internal–external alignment (people management, EVP coherence)

- Cultural context and generational shifts: EB content that fits one culture or cohort can turn off others, leading to narrower pools and missed targets. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity is needed; EB effectiveness depends on accuracy and appeal that varies by audience</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-4">Understanding what appeals to job searchers is crucial in severe talent shortages; attractiveness and accuracy determine EB success</cite>.

- Halo/transfer failure: Candidates infer job desirability from general employer attractiveness (e.g., innovative culture) but the specific role requires analytical rigor or compliance; the EB-driven “fit” is misdirected, producing lower quality applicants and slower conversion to hires. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants’ attraction decisions rely on attractiveness factors like prestige and innovation</cite> <cite id="43896364-3">Attraction requires integrating building blocks so that employer attractiveness is tailored and job‑linked</cite>.

- Expectation-state distortion: In tight markets, generic EB can raise de‑sired applications from overqualified aspirants who expect premium bundles; when offers are rejected or bundles are constrained, time-to-fill and attrition worsen. <cite id="b318d47e-4">EB is an enticement in tight markets but effective attraction remains elusive without alignment</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and signal content shape attraction decisions, so misaligned EB under scarcity reduces effective applications</cite>.
- Homogenization and diversity risks: EB that emphasizes “cool culture” or sector cachet can attract similar, highly filtered cohorts, narrowing diversity and reducing functional fit for specialized roles. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Sector and culture act as signals; attraction to the public vs. private sector differs</cite> <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity and audience-specific appeal are necessary; inattention increases risk of biased pools</cite>.

- Market tightness and talent scarcity: Tight markets amplify both the upside and downside of EB—more applications at greater cost, with higher risks of expectation gaps and de‑motivation if EB overpromises or lacks specificity. <cite id="b318d47e-4">EB’s enticement role intensifies under tight markets, yet many firms still struggle with effective attraction</cite> <cite id="b318d47e-0">Organizations that fail to realign EB under scarcity lose the talent race</cite>.
- Sector and institutional context: Public vs. private/nonprofit signals differ; EB must reflect sector realities to attract the right pools. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants’ attraction to the public sector is smaller than private/nonprofit in many contexts; sector acts as a signal</cite>.
- Cultural and generational context: Cultural biases in perceived image and Gen Z’s social media–mediated decisions require tailored, accurate messaging to avoid misfit and disillusionment. <cite id="ca1e7319-4">Cultural sensitivity and accurate, appealing messaging are critical; EB success depends on attractiveness and accuracy</cite>.
- EB program integrity: Presence of differentiated EVP, people management strategy parity, and brand consistency increases the odds EB improves outcomes; absence increases the odds EB worsens them. <cite id="43896364-2">Differentiated EVP, people management, brand consistency, communication, and metrics are building blocks for predicting attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="43896364-3">An integrated approach linking building blocks to attraction and retention is necessary</cite>.

Signals that EB is likely to harm outcomes
- EB messaging focuses on aspirational culture or prestige without specifying how the role contributes to those outcomes. <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicants rely on prestige/innovation cues, but these must be tied to concrete job appraisals</cite>.
- EB content and internal practices diverge (e.g., “innovative” brand with rigid hierarchy or “flexible” myth without real autonomy). <cite id="b318d47e-0">Failure to realign EB with internal realities undermines attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="43896364-2">Brand consistency and people management strategy are core</cite>.
- EB is generic across roles and audiences; segmentation by target group needs is absent. <cite id="43896364-2">Target group needs and segmentation are a key building block for predicting attraction</cite>.

Evidence strength and gaps
- The literature consistently shows EB can increase intention to apply and retention when grounded in a differentiated, authentic EVP, coherent people practices, and audience segmentation; deviations predict misfit, skepticism, and poor conversion. <cite id="b318d47e-0">Evidence supports EB–attraction links, but effectiveness hinges on correct development and realignment</cite> <cite id="43896364-1">Predictive models integrate building blocks to explain EB’s causal links to attraction and retention</cite> <cite id="4bc37c03-0">Applicant attraction responds to sector- and culture-linked signals</cite>.
- Direct field-experimental estimates of EB backfire magnitudes are sparse in these sources; stronger causal evidence would include randomized EB message tests measuring intention-to-apply, application quality, and offer acceptance across labor market tightness and demographic segments. <cite id="4bc37c03-4">Accuracy and attractiveness as EB metrics are emphasized, implying the need for measurable, audience-tailored evaluation</cite>.

Bottom line
EB worsens talent attraction when it markets generic prestige/culture without job-specific value, hides misalignments behind inauthentic narratives, or is deployed without segmenting target needs—especially under tight labor markets and cultural contexts where signals are misread. The quest to win the talent war has expanded to employer brand issues deemed to be related to the attraction and retention of talented staff (Bussin, 2007;Crous, 2007;Dell et al., 2001;Hallén, 2007;Lawler, 2000;Minchington, 2010;Prinsloo, 2008;Zingheim & Schuster, 2000). The impact of persistent talent shortage could render organisations incapable of growth, and detract from their efficacy in gaining or sustaining a winning edge, thus ultimately jeopardising their survival (Boshard & Louw, 2010;Charest, 2011;Prinsloo, 2008). The collapse of organisations adversely affects the macroeconomic environment as it counters sustainable economic growth, which in turn negatively influences a better quality life for all. 

The need for employer brand models, which could be empirically tested to successfully predict talent attraction and retention, motivated this study. Benefits of models are underscored by Mouton (2001) who states models allow one to make predictive claims under certain conditions, and bring conceptual coherence to a domain of science thereby simplifying our understanding of the world. Thus, models limit, isolate, simplify and systematise the domain that is investigated, and provide explanation sketches and the means for making predictions (Jordaan, 2007). 

The aim of this study is to present an employer brand predictive model with building blocks that denote an integrated approach which shapes and influences the total employer brand process relative to talent attraction and retention. It is hoped that this employer brand predictive model will provide managers and human resource functionaries guidance on more effective employer brand decisions that will mitigate talent limitations and bolster overall business performance.

The transition from the industrial era to the knowledge era has changed the employer-employee relationship paradigm, and the supply and demand curve for talent is becoming increasingly favoured towards the talented employee. The quest to win the talent war confronts companies around the world to realign their employer brand efforts in a bid to mitigate talent limitations (Deloitte LLP, 2010;Minchington, 2006). 

Employer brand is associated with an organisation's differentiated attractiveness in terms of functional, economic and psychological benefits (Ambler & Barrow, 1996;Corporate Leadership Council, 2007;Donath, 2001;Minchington, 2006) and a strong employer brand acts as an enticement for talent in the current marketplace (Rosethorn, 2009;Willock, 2005). Talent refers to an individual's differentiated potential or ability to execute against the organisation's growth strategy and is a term that is much talked about in the contemporary era, however, effective talent attraction and retention remains an elusive business feat (Boshard & Louw, 2010;Charest, 2011;Cheese et al., 2007;Leonardi, 2007;Personnel Today, 2008;Prinsloo, 2008). 

Although research evidence supports the relationship between employer brand and the attraction and retention of talent, limited attempts have been undertaken to identify employer brand concepts in the format of an employer brand model, that predicts talent attraction and retention (Armstrong, 2007;Backhaus & Tikoo, 2004;Crous, 2007;Dell et al., 2001;Jenner & Taylor, 2007;Martin, 2007;Minchington, 2010;Willock, 2005). 

These trends highlighted the need for empirically validated employer brand models that can predict effective talent attraction and retention efforts, and provide a coherent view that explains employer brand concepts contributing to talent attraction and retention.

Why would someone really good at their job want to join your company? And how will you keep them for more than a few years? Against the background of these contemporary questions, and at a time when seeking talent in the ever shrinking global talent pool has become an international crusade, companies are uncertain as to what talent attraction and retention decisions they should be making (Armstrong, 2007;Bussin, 2007;Crous, 2007;Leonardi, 2007;Minchington, 2006). 

A growing body of research evidence supports the relationship between employer brand and the attraction and retention of talent (Cheese, Thomas & Craig, 2007;Crous, 2007;Minchington, 2010;Willock, 2005). Even though it is fairly customary amongst larger companies to use employer brand to attract and retain talent (Dell, Ainspan, Bodenberg, Troy & Hickey, 2001), companies are ineffective in developing, maintaining or realigning their employer brand efforts correctly thereby losing out on a powerful talent attraction and retention tool (Cheese et al., 2007;Minchington, 2006). 

Most employer brand research focuses on the possible relationship between various employer brand concepts and talent attraction and retention, with limited attempts to build a coherent employer brand model that can successfully predict talent attraction and retention. The key focus of this study is to integrate relevant employer brand concepts, or employer brand building blocks, in an employer brand predictive model that can be empirically validated to predict talent attraction and retention.

Title: An employer brand predictive model for talent attraction and retention : original research
Snippet: The purpose of this study was to explore the current state of knowledge about employer brand and to identify employer brand building blocks that can be integrated in an employer brand predictive model that will predict talent attraction and retention after being empirically validated. 

During the initial literature overview key employer brand concepts were isolated due to researchers' significance attributed to these concepts in relation to talent attraction and retention. These employer brand concepts were refined to the following keywords: target group needs and/or segmentation, differentiated EVP, people management strategy, brand consistency, employer brand communication and HR employer branding metrics. These keywords were used to inform a comprehensive literature review that resulted in six propositions. Thereafter these same keywords were applied to guide research that would either support or reject the propositions. 

Given the fact that the research findings reiterated the stated propositions, these propositions served as a guide to determine the following building blocks of an employer brand predictive model that can be empirically validated to effectively predict talent attraction and retention, and contribute to favourable positioning in the quest for talent: 

• Target group needs  The model presented in Figure 1 is theoretical in nature and a form of inductive reasoning, or conceptual explication, was used to search for linkages between theoretical concepts. Even though there is criticism of inductive reasoning because of its qualitative nature, it remains one of the most powerful methods to construct conceptual models and build new theories, without which science cannot make progress (Mouton, 2001). As stated in a previous section of this study, theoretical models allow one to make predictive claims under certain conditions, and bring conceptual coherence to a domain of science thereby simplifying our understanding of the world (Mouton, 2001). The employer brand predictive model limited, isolated, simplified and systematised the employer brand domain that was investigated, thereby adding value to scientific progress though the accurate representation of a set of phenomena, and propositions, which can be empirically tested.

Title: An employer brand predictive model for talent attraction and retention : original research
Snippet: This study was embedded in the search for linkages between theoretical concepts, and allowed the researcher to make predictive claims and bring conceptual coherence by explaining links between propositions. The aim was to determine building blocks of an employer brand predictive model and understand how these building blocks integrate to form a conceptual coherence that depicts employer brand relative to talent attraction and retention.

Snippet: Why would someone really good at their job want to join your company? And how will you keep them for more than a few years? Against the background of these contemporary questions, and at a time when seeking talent in the ever shrinking global talent pool has become an international crusade, companies are uncertain as to what talent attraction and retention decisions they should be making (Armstrong, 2007;Bussin, 2007;Crous, 2007;Leonardi, 2007;Minchington, 2006). 

A growing body of research evidence supports the relationship between employer brand and the attraction and retention of talent (Cheese, Thomas & Craig, 2007;Crous, 2007;Minchington, 2010;Willock, 2005). Even though it is fairly customary amongst larger companies to use employer brand to attract and retain talent (Dell, Ainspan, Bodenberg, Troy & Hickey, 2001), companies are ineffective in developing, maintaining or realigning their employer brand efforts correctly thereby losing out on a powerful talent attraction and retention tool (Cheese et al., 2007;Minchington, 2006). 

Most employer brand research focuses on the possible relationship between various employer brand concepts and talent attraction and retention, with limited attempts to build a coherent employer brand model that can successfully predict talent attraction and retention. The key focus of this study is to integrate relevant employer brand concepts, or employer brand building blocks, in an employer brand predictive model that can be empirically validated to predict talent attraction and retention.

Title: The Relationship Between Internal Employer Branding and Talent Retention: A Theoretical Investigation for the Development of a Conceptual Framework
Snippet: We postulate that the antecedent of employer branding, such as job design, competitive compensation, organizational environment, career progression, and employers' prestige, causes to build employer brand image that eventually causes employees engagement and talent retention. The construct of employer brand image and employee engagement plays mediating role between antecedents of employer branding and talent retention. In the proposed conceptual framework, all relationships are rightly/positively causing their effects. It addresses novelty through the addition of job design as the antecedent of employer branding and the double mediation through employer brand image and employees' engagement. On the basis of reviewed literature of employer brand image, employees' engagement, and talent retention, it is conceptualized that competitive compensation (Chhabra and Sharma, 2014;Carpentier et al., 2017;Sharma and Prasad, 2018;Deepa and Baral, 2019), organizational environment (Jain and Bhatt, 2015;Stokes, 2015;Saraswathy and Balakrishnan, 2017;Urbancova et al., 2017;Kaur et al., 2018;Sageder et al., 2018;Sharma and Prasad, 2018;Deepa and Baral, 2019), career progression (Barrow and Mosley, 2007;Vaiman, 2008;Minchington, 2010;Priyadarshi, 2011;Truss et al., 2012;Dessler, 2016), organization's prestige (Urde and Greyser, 2016;Carpentier et al., 2017;Saraswathy and Balakrishnan, 2017;Sharma and Prasad, 2018), and job design (Carpentier et al., 2017) have theoretical relationship with attitudinal variable employer brand image, which is theoretically linked with behavioral variable, i.e., mediator between attitude and consequence employees' engagement (Kahn, 1990;Schaufeli et al., 2002;Inceoglu and Warr, 2012;Wang, 2016;Vorina et al., 2017), which has further theoretical relationship with behavioral consequences, talent retention at will (Arasanmi and Krishna, 2019;Qureshi, 2019;West et al., 2019). Hence, the final conceptual framework is depicted in Figure 2.

Title: An employer brand predictive model for talent attraction and retention : original research
Snippet: The transition from the industrial era to the knowledge era has changed the employer-employee relationship paradigm, and the supply and demand curve for talent is becoming increasingly favoured towards the talented employee. The quest to win the talent war confronts companies around the world to realign their employer brand efforts in a bid to mitigate talent limitations (Deloitte LLP, 2010;Minchington, 2006). 

Employer brand is associated with an organisation's differentiated attractiveness in terms of functional, economic and psychological benefits (Ambler & Barrow, 1996;Corporate Leadership Council, 2007;Donath, 2001;Minchington, 2006) and a strong employer brand acts as an enticement for talent in the current marketplace (Rosethorn, 2009;Willock, 2005). Talent refers to an individual's differentiated potential or ability to execute against the organisation's growth strategy and is a term that is much talked about in the contemporary era, however, effective talent attraction and retention remains an elusive business feat (Boshard & Louw, 2010;Charest, 2011;Cheese et al., 2007;Leonardi, 2007;Personnel Today, 2008;Prinsloo, 2008). 

Although research evidence supports the relationship between employer brand and the attraction and retention of talent, limited attempts have been undertaken to identify employer brand concepts in the format of an employer brand model, that predicts talent attraction and retention (Armstrong, 2007;Backhaus & Tikoo, 2004;Crous, 2007;Dell et al., 2001;Jenner & Taylor, 2007;Martin, 2007;Minchington, 2010;Willock, 2005). 

These trends highlighted the need for empirically validated employer brand models that can predict effective talent attraction and retention efforts, and provide a coherent view that explains employer brand concepts contributing to talent attraction and retention.

Title: The Relationship Between Internal Employer Branding and Talent Retention: A Theoretical Investigation for the Development of a Conceptual Framework
Snippet: The phenomenon of employer branding (Barrow and Mosley, 2007;Priyadarshi, 2011;Carpentier et al., 2017;Saraswathy and Balakrishnan, 2017;Urbancova et al., 2017;Astrachan et al., 2018;Kaur et al., 2018;Sageder et al., 2018;Sharma and Prasad, 2018;Deepa and Baral, 2019) along with its antecedents and its consequence employees' engagement (Kahn, 1990;Schaufeli et al., 2002;Inceoglu and Warr, 2012;Warr and Inceoglu, 2012;Wang, 2016;Vorina et al., 2017), talent retention at will (Arasanmi and Krishna, 2019;Qureshi, 2019;West et al., 2019) has been explored and explained through different research studies but intensive literature review lacks empirical shreds of evidence of theoretical relationship among all three constructs, i.e., employer branding, employee's engagement, and talent retention in one particular social setting, which means theoretical gap exists in the literature. Job design (Okolo et al., 2018;Kamel, 2019) has been explained as an antecedent of employees' engagement and talent retention, but literature review lacks sound evidence where it has been considered as an antecedent of employer brand image and having mediation effect on it, i.e., employer brand image with two consequences, e.g., employees' engagement and talent retention. Therefore, a theoretical gap exists in the extant literature. 

Since the emergence of cultural dimensions back in 1981, Hofstede ( 2011) explored nine cultural dimensions on the basis of which one social setting is different from others. Without testing in the specific social setting, research studies and phenomena testified in other social settings might not bring the same results. The triangular relationship of employer branding, employees' engagement, and employees' talent retention needs to be testified in different social settings before generalizing and practicing.

Title: An employer brand predictive model for talent attraction and retention : original research
Snippet: At a time when seeking talent in the ever shrinking global talent pool has become an international crusade (Armstrong, 2007;Bussin, 2007;Crous, 2007;Leonardi, 2007;Minchington, 2006), the quest to win the talent war has expanded to HR best practice, employer brand, reward, recognition and benefits -all issues related to the attraction and retention of talented staff (Crous, 2007). 

Employer brand is defined as the organisation's differentiated attractiveness in terms of functional, economic and psychological benefits that are identified with the image of the employing company (Ambler & Barrow, 1996;Corporate Leadership Council, 2007;Donath, 2001;Minchington, 2006). 

Although a growing body of evidence supports the relationship between employer brand and the attraction and retention of talent (Crous, 2007;Dell et al., 2001;Minchington, 2010;Willock, 2005), limited attempts to build an employer brand model to predict talent attraction and retention has been undertaken (Armstrong, 2007;Backhaus & Tikoo, 2004;Jenner & Taylor, 2007;Martin, 2007). The purpose of this study was to explore the current state of knowledge about employer brand and to determine the key building blocks of an employer brand predictive model that can be empirically validated to effectively predict talent attraction and retention. 

The benefit of the study's model building approach systemises the employer brand domain and brings conceptual coherence to a domain of science. Another contribution of the study is providing managers and human resource functionaries an integrated approach which shapes and influences the total employer brand process relative to talent attraction and retention. The following discussion synthesises linkages in literature between theoretical concepts and explains causal links between propositions.

Title: Employer branding dimensions: An adapted scale for Eastern Europe
Snippet: The authors found that employees considered their organisation's employer brand to be more attractive when the organisation was perceived to be successful, when they valued the attributes of the organisation's product or service, and when they construed its external image as being attractive.Many of the latter aspects, Maxwell and Knox (2009) suggest, are culturally biased.Our results indeed respond to calls for the cultural sensitivity of employer branding activities (Sivertzen et al., 2013).The evidence provided here shows positive associations between employer attractiveness and the likelihood of job satisfaction.This finding highlights the internal side effects strong employer branding activities may be able to generate.Hence, our findings are also in line with research by Backhaus and Tikoo (2004) and Martin et al. (2011).

Future research direction might also consider studies with highly knowledgeable employees at different stages in their career (junior or senior practitioners) to better understand how they perceive their work and the employer brand.Depending upon career stage this work would link to extant attraction-selection attribution/personorganisation fit theory, but would need to address the potential paradox that if being a 'strong' employer brand involves attracting and retaining the most talented employees within the organisation (and all such employees are potentially highly skilled and knowledgeable), who will undertake more mundane jobs?Similarly, loss of such talented employees may influence the employer brand that may be explored, and this could be the objective of future research.By drawing on an existing measure we may have overlooked other cultural aspects that may enrich the conceptual domain of employer attractiveness.Future research can therefore focus on qualitive, depth interviews with employers, and/or employees that could then lead to new employer branding dimensions.
